meta.title: Benzodiazepines app: domain data
meta.note: Single source of the domain data used and shown by the app: drug, molecular, receptor, route, regional and model data. Values are approximate, rounded literature-range figures for teaching; edit here to correct them. Colours stored with items are their display colours.

units.subunits.*.gabaEC50: GABA EC50 at the alpha-beta-gamma2 receptor (uM)
units.drugs.*.smiles: SMILES (used to draw the 2D structure, tools/build_structures.py)
units.drugs.*.pd.emax: cooperativity factor beta: maximal fold-shift of GABA EC50 (>1 PAM, 1 neutral antagonist, <1 inverse agonist)
units.drugs.*.pd.ki: Ki per alpha isoform (nM); null = no measurable binding (BZD-insensitive)
units.drugs.*.pk.ref: therapeutic or reference plasma range [low, high] (ng/mL); null = not defined
units.drugs.*.pk.pathways: fraction of clearance by pathway (cyp3a4, cyp2c19, ugt, other); sums to 1
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites: active metabolites: fm (fraction of parent formed), t12 (h), vd (L/kg), pathways; mw: molecular weight (g/mol, PubChem), used for molar units
units.modifiers.*.m: multiplier on clearance by pathway (patient factor or interaction)
units.modifiers.*.vLipo: multiplier on Vd of lipophilic drugs
units.subunits.*: alpha isoforms: label, gabaEC50 (uM), BZD sensitivity, determinant residue, effects, distribution, clinical relevance
units.drugs.*.pd.kind: mechanism at the BZD site (PAM, Partial PAM, Antagonist, Inverse agonist)
units.drugRoutes.<drug>.<route>: clinical speed category, onset of action, Tmax (text ranges), indications, advantages and cautions
units.regions.abundance.<isoform>.<region>: relative abundance level (0 absent or trace, 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high) and the cell populations concerned
units.model.singleChannel: Cl- and HCO3- flux readout (GHK current equation): single-channel conductance (pS) measured in symmetrical Cl- (symmetricCl_mM); extracellular and intracellular Cl- (mM) in mature neurons (clIn_mM) and immature neurons (clInImmature_mM); default membrane potential and the limits of its slider (vmMin_mV, vmMax_mV; mV); temperature (deg C); extracellular and intracellular HCO3- (mM) and the HCO3-/Cl- permeability ratio; E_Cl, E_HCO3 (Nernst) and E_GABA (GHK voltage equation) follow from these
units.model.kinetics: kinetic (Markov) scheme of the alpha1beta3gamma2L receptor (Haas & Macdonald 1999, Fig. 7, rates as corrected in the 2004 erratum), recorded at temperatureLow_C-temperatureHigh_C (deg C). States: C1 unbound, C2 one GABA bound, C3 and C4 two bound (closed); O1 (from C2), O2 (from C3), O3 (from C4); desensitised Df (from C3), Di (from C4), Ds (from Di); distal brief closed states C5-C10, two per open state. Rates in 1/s except kon (1/(M s)): C1->C2 2*kon*[GABA], C2->C1 koff, C2->C3 kon*[GABA], C3->C2 2*koff, C3<->C4 k34/k43, open (beta) and close (alpha) rates per open state, df/rf, di/ri, ds/rs; a12o/b12o: rates from the two distal closed states back to O1 and O2, a12c/b12c: rates from O1 and O2 into them; a3o, b3o, a3c, b3c the same for O3. BZD-site ligands multiply kon by the EC50 shift of the allosteric model
units.model.ipsc: simulated IPSC: control peak amplitude (pA), effective peak synaptic GABA (uM; sets the amplitude change with the allosteric shift), rise time constant (ms), fast and slow decay time constants (ms) and the fraction of the fast component; decay time constants are multiplied by shift^decayShiftExponent
units.model.routeDefaults: absorption (F, ka 1/h) used when a drug has no route-specific data
units.model.doseResponse: dose-effect figure: GABA tone (uM), subunit, BZD concentration at 1x dose as a multiple of Ki, opioid effect and synergy, barbiturate constants, effect bands (% of max)
units.model.durationComparison: drugs and oral doses (mg) in the duration-of-action comparison
units.routes[]: administration routes: onset, onsetMin (representative onset in min, used for bar length), Tmax, bioavailability, indications, advantages, limitations
units.references: literature cited by the data, checked against PubMed (authors, year, title, journal, volume, pages, pmid, doi); FDA labels carry setid and url (DailyMed)
units.sources: source of each value, keyed by its path in this file: refs (ids in references), reported (value reported in the source), status (consistent = within the reported value or range; differs = outside it; full text = cited, value still to be checked against the full text; model = teaching parameter of the model; calibrated = fitted to the calibration data in "validation"), note
units.sourceChecks: settings for tools/check_sources.py: path of the Ki values in each drug, tolerated fold difference, ChEMBL target ids and Guide to Pharmacology target names per subunit, species
units.validation: observed single-dose peak plasma concentrations in adults: set (calibration = used to fit ka; validation = independent studies, not used for fitting), drug, route, dose (mg), cmax (ng/mL) and tmax (h), each a value or [low, high] range, refs, note; tmaxUpper = the reported Tmax is an upper bound ("peak within ...")
units.jurisdictions: region-specific values: us (base data, FDA labels, US brands) and eu (overlay of values that differ in EU SmPCs as published in FASS, Swedish product names); concentrationUnit is the plasma concentration unit shown (ng/mL and µg/L are numerically equal); data is merged over the base data when the region is selected; se inherits the eu values and shows plasma concentrations in nmol/L, converted with each molecular weight: nmol/L = ng/mL × 1000 / MW

a1.label: α1
a1.effect: Sedation, anterograde amnesia, part of anticonvulsant action, ataxia
a1.location: ~60% of brain GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors · cortex, thalamus, cerebellum (synaptic)
a1.clinical: Target of α1-preferring hypnotics (zolpidem); mediates the main dose-limiting adverse effects (sedation, psychomotor impairment, falls) and is implicated in reinforcement and dependence.

a2.label: α2
a2.clinical: Considered the principal mediator of BZD anxiolysis; the rationale for α2/α3-selective PAMs developed as non-sedating anxiolytics and analgesics.

a3.label: α3
a3.clinical: With α2, a target for non-sedating anxiolytics; contributes to spinal antihyperalgesia relevant to chronic pain.

a5.label: α5
a5.effect: Learning & memory; contributes to amnesia and tolerance to sedation
a5.clinical: α5-selective negative modulators (e.g. basmisanil) have been investigated as cognitive enhancers.

a4.label: α4
a4.effect: BZD-insensitive · tonic inhibition (often with δ); neurosteroid-sensitive and a proposed low-dose ethanol target
a4.clinical: Unaffected by flumazenil; extrasynaptic α4βδ receptors are a target of neurosteroids (cf. brexanolone and zuranolone in postpartum depression).

a6.label: α6
a6.clinical: Not targeted by clinically used BZDs; contributes to cerebellar motor coordination and ethanol sensitivity.

otherSubunits.label: β2/3
facts: principal (+) face of both GABA sites (β+/α−)
β2 Tyr97, Tyr157, Phe200, Tyr205 (GABA binding)
not involved; low-affinity TMD sites at µM diazepam
otherSubunits.effect: Required for receptor assembly and for GABA binding and gating
otherSubunits.clinical: β+/α− transmembrane sites mediate general anaesthetics: β3 N265M knock-in mice lose the immobilising action of propofol and etomidate, and β2 N265S mice lose the sedative action of etomidate. Not targeted by clinical BZD doses.
otherSubunits.location: Present in virtually all GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors; β2 most abundant, β3 prominent in cortex, hippocampus and striatum

otherSubunits.label: γ2
facts: complementary (−) face of the BZD site (α+/γ2−)
otherSubunits.effect: Confers high-affinity BZD sensitivity, increases single-channel conductance and mediates postsynaptic clustering via gephyrin
otherSubunits.clinical: γ2 F77I knock-in mice are insensitive to zolpidem; GABRG2 variants cause genetic epilepsies (e.g. GEFS+, febrile seizures). Receptors lacking γ2 do not respond to BZDs or flumazenil.
otherSubunits.location: Widespread; the majority of synaptic receptors (α1/2/3βγ2)

otherSubunits.label: δ
facts: replaces γ2: α4βδ, α6βδ (and α1βδ) receptors
otherSubunits.effect: Mediates tonic (extrasynaptic) inhibition that sets neuronal excitability
otherSubunits.clinical: Target of neurosteroids (allopregnanolone; brexanolone and zuranolone in postpartum depression) and of gaboxadol; proposed site of low-dose ethanol action. Classical BZDs and flumazenil have no effect.
otherSubunits.location: Dentate gyrus granule cells and thalamus (with α4), cerebellar granule cells (with α6)

diazepam.name: Diazepam
diazepam.use: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, muscle spasm

midazolam.name: Midazolam
midazolam.use: Procedural sedation, anaesthesia induction, status epilepticus

zopiclone.name: Zopiclone
zopiclone.use: Insomnia (cyclopyrrolone "Z-drug"; binds α1/2/3/5 without zolpidem-like α1 preference)

bretazenil.name: Bretazenil
bretazenil.use: High-affinity imidazopyrrolobenzodiazepine partial agonist - lower ceiling effect & reduced dependence

dmcm.name: DMCM
dmcm.use: β-carboline; anxiogenic & proconvulsant - reduces GABA affinity

gaba.name: GABA
gaba.use: γ-aminobutyric acid · binds two orthosteric β+/α− sites and gates the Cl⁻ pore

routes.name: Intravenous (IV)
routes.primaryIndications: Status epilepticus, acute procedural sedation, rapid induction of anaesthesia
routes.advantages: Immediate systemic bio-availability; exact dose titration possible
routes.limitations: High risk of respiratory depression, apnoea, hypotension, thrombophlebitis (diazepam vehicle)

routes.name: Intranasal (IN)
routes.primaryIndications: Out-of-hospital seizure clusters, acute agitation when IV line cannot be placed
routes.advantages: Rapid mucosal absorption directly entering systemic circulation; bypasses GI tract and first pass
routes.limitations: Nasal congestion/rhinitis may diminish absorption; nasal discomfort and stinging

routes.name: Buccal
routes.primaryIndications: Paediatric prolonged acute convulsive seizures (first-line in emergency protocols)
routes.advantages: Non-invasive mucosal delivery; simple for parents and caregivers to administer safely
routes.limitations: Portion may be swallowed into GI tract; active salivation/swallowing alters uptake

routes.name: Rectal
routes.primaryIndications: Paediatric emergency seizure rescue; febrile status epilepticus when IV unavailable
routes.advantages: Viable when patient is actively convulsing or unconscious with no venous access
routes.limitations: Social/privacy stigma in older patients; variable absorption depending on rectal contents

routes.name: Sublingual (SL)
routes.primaryIndications: Acute panic attacks, severe situational anxiety, anticipatory anxiety
routes.advantages: Faster onset than swallowed tablets; partially avoids hepatic first-pass extraction; no water needed
routes.limitations: Requires patient cooperation to hold under tongue without swallowing; dry mouth slows dissolution

routes.name: Intramuscular (IM)
routes.primaryIndications: Severe behavioural agitation, pre-anaesthetic medication, acute psychiatric emergency
routes.advantages: Rapid and predictable absorption for water-soluble/propylene glycol formulations (Midazolam, Lorazepam)
routes.limitations: Diazepam precipitates in muscle tissue due to lipophilicity causing slow/erratic absorption and pain

routes.name: Oral (PO)
routes.commonDrugs: Virtually all BZDs & Z-drugs (Diazepam, Lorazepam, Alprazolam, Clonazepam, etc.)
routes.primaryIndications: Generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, insomnia, spasticity, chronic maintenance
routes.advantages: Most convenient for self-administration and chronic outpatient therapy; non-invasive
routes.limitations: Delayed onset; influenced by gastric emptying and food; substantial first-pass for midazolam/triazolam
routes.bioavailability: Diazepam or Lorazepam or Clonazepam > 85-90%; Midazolam ~40%; Triazolam ~50%

oral.ind: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal and muscle spasm; adjunct in seizure disorders
oral.adv: Rapid and near-complete oral absorption (F ≈ 95%); long duration through nordiazepam allows once-daily dosing and smooth tapering
oral.caut: Nordiazepam accumulates with repeated dosing (t½ up to 200 h), particularly in older adults, in hepatic impairment and with CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inhibitors

rectal.ind: Acute repetitive or prolonged seizures out of hospital, particularly in children, when IV access is unavailable
rectal.adv: Can be given by trained caregivers; high bioavailability (≈ 90%)
rectal.caut: Variable absorption; respiratory depression with repeated doses; less acceptable than buccal or intranasal routes in older children and adults

nasal.ind: Intermittent seizure clusters (acute repetitive seizures) in epilepsy
nasal.adv: Easy caregiver administration with high bioavailability of the nasal formulation; avoids rectal use
nasal.caut: Nasal discomfort and dysgeusia; respiratory depression, particularly with opioids or other CNS depressants

im.ind: Not recommended; reserve for situations in which no other route is available
im.adv: None over alternatives: IM midazolam or IM lorazepam is preferred
im.caut: Slow and erratic absorption because of poor aqueous solubility; injection-site pain

iv.ind: Status epilepticus, severe alcohol withdrawal and procedural sedation
iv.adv: Onset within minutes owing to high lipid solubility and rapid brain uptake
iv.caut: Short anticonvulsant effect because of redistribution, with risk of seizure recurrence; respiratory depression and hypotension; thrombophlebitis from the propylene glycol vehicle

oral.ind: Panic disorder; short-term treatment of generalised anxiety disorder
oral.caut: Interdose rebound anxiety and high dependence and withdrawal risk; CYP3A4 inhibitors increase exposure

sl.adv: Taken without water; partial avoidance of first-pass metabolism and slightly faster absorption
sl.caut: Same dependence and withdrawal risks as oral alprazolam; sublingual use is off-label in many countries

oral.ind: Short-term treatment of anxiety, insomnia associated with anxiety, and premedication
oral.adv: No active metabolites; direct glucuronidation is preserved in hepatic impairment and in older adults
oral.caut: Slower oral peak (≈ 2 h) than diazepam; anterograde amnesia; dependence with prolonged use

sl.ind: Acute anxiety or panic attacks; premedication
sl.adv: High bioavailability (≈ 94%) with an earlier peak than oral tablets; no swallowing required
sl.caut: Requires patient cooperation; onset slower than intranasal or buccal midazolam

im.ind: Status epilepticus or acute agitation when IV access is unavailable; premedication
im.caut: Slower peak than IM midazolam, which is generally preferred for seizures without IV access

iv.ind: First-line treatment of status epilepticus; acute agitation; alcohol withdrawal
iv.adv: Longer anticonvulsant effect than IV diazepam (less redistribution), reducing seizure recurrence
iv.caut: Respiratory depression and hypotension; propylene glycol toxicity with high-dose or prolonged infusion; requires refrigeration

oral.ind: Seizure disorders (absence, myoclonic, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome); panic disorder
oral.adv: Long half-life (30-40 h) allows once- or twice-daily dosing
oral.caut: Tolerance to the anticonvulsant effect; sedation and accumulation; hypersalivation in children

iv.ind: Status epilepticus where an IV formulation is available
iv.adv: Potent, with a longer anticonvulsant effect than IV diazepam
iv.caut: Respiratory depression and hypotension; not available in all countries (e.g. not in the USA)

oral.ind: Premedication and procedural sedation, particularly in children (oral solution)
oral.adv: Rapid onset and short duration (t½ 1.5-3 h)
oral.caut: Low and variable bioavailability (≈ 40%) from CYP3A4 first-pass metabolism; large increases with CYP3A4 inhibitors and in hepatic impairment

buccal.ind: Prolonged acute convulsive seizures in infants, children and adolescents
buccal.adv: First-line out-of-hospital rescue: easy caregiver administration, more acceptable and at least as effective as rectal diazepam
buccal.caut: Part of the dose may be swallowed, reducing the effect; respiratory depression, particularly with repeated doses

nasal.ind: Intermittent seizure clusters in patients aged 12 years and older
nasal.caut: Nasal discomfort, rhinorrhoea and dysgeusia; bioavailability ≈ 45-55%; respiratory depression

im.ind: Status epilepticus without IV access (pre-hospital first line); acute agitation; premedication
im.adv: Water-soluble at acidic pH, giving rapid and reliable IM absorption; at least as effective as IV lorazepam before hospital arrival (RAMPART trial)
im.caut: Respiratory depression, particularly in older adults or with other CNS depressants

iv.ind: Procedural sedation, induction of anaesthesia, ICU sedation; continuous infusion in refractory status epilepticus
iv.adv: Rapid onset and offset; readily titrated
iv.caut: Apnoea, respiratory depression and hypotension; accumulation of the active glucuronide in renal impairment and with prolonged infusion

oral.ind: Anxiety; alcohol withdrawal, particularly in hepatic impairment
oral.adv: No active metabolites; direct glucuronidation is largely preserved in liver disease and in older adults
oral.caut: Slow absorption makes it unsuitable for acute use; dosing three to four times daily

oral.adv: Rapid onset and short duration with little next-day residual effect
oral.caut: Rebound insomnia, anterograde amnesia and next-day anxiety; contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole)

sl.ind: Procedural or dental anxiolysis (off-label sublingual use)
sl.adv: Higher bioavailability and faster onset than oral tablets by partially avoiding first-pass metabolism
sl.caut: Off-label use; requires monitoring, particularly in combination with other sedatives

oral.adv: Rapid onset and short half-life (2-3 h); less myorelaxation than BZDs at therapeutic doses
oral.caut: FDA boxed warning (2019) for complex sleep behaviours; next-morning impairment (lower doses for women); dependence

sl.ind: Sleep-onset insomnia, and middle-of-the-night awakening (low-dose sublingual tablets)
sl.adv: Faster absorption than the oral tablet
sl.caut: Take low-dose tablets only when at least 4 h remain in bed; complex sleep behaviours (FDA boxed warning)

oral.ind: Short-term treatment of insomnia (sleep onset and maintenance)
oral.adv: Improves sleep onset and maintenance, with a moderate half-life (5-6 h)
oral.caut: Bitter metallic taste; next-day impairment; complex sleep behaviours (FDA boxed warning for eszopiclone); dependence

oral.ind: None approved; investigated as an anxiolytic and anticonvulsant
oral.adv: Partial agonist with a lower ceiling effect, expected to cause less sedation and dependence
oral.caut: Not marketed; clinical development was discontinued

iv.ind: Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after procedures; selected cases of isolated benzodiazepine overdose
iv.caut: Short half-life (≈ 1 h) with risk of resedation; can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or with tricyclic co-ingestion; not for routine use in undifferentiated overdose

pathways.name: Diazepam: multi-branch metabolic cascade
pathways.note: Multiple active metabolites with very long elimination half-lives lead to pronounced cumulative effects during chronic dosing.

pathways.name: Direct glucuronidation (LOT benzodiazepines)
pathways.note: Lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam bypass phase I cytochrome P450 oxidation, which favours their use in older adults and in hepatic impairment.

pathways.name: Midazolam: rapid hydroxylation pathway
pathways.note: Extensive intestinal and hepatic first-pass extraction (~60%) and rapid conversion to the short-lived active metabolite 1′-hydroxymidazolam.

cyp3a4_inh.label: CYP3A4 inhibitor
cyp3a4_inh.desc: e.g. ketoconazole, clarithromycin · reduces 3A4 clearance by 70%

cyp2c19_pm.label: CYP2C19 poor metaboliser
cyp2c19_pm.desc: Common genetic polymorphism (~15-20% in Asian populations) · reduces diazepam clearance

elderly.label: Older adult (≥ 65 y)
elderly.desc: Decreased Phase I hepatic oxidation (~40%) and expanded Vd for lipophilic drugs (+30%). Phase II UGT preserved.

cirrhosis.label: Severe liver disease
cirrhosis.desc: Shunting and loss of functional hepatocytes · Phase I heavily impaired (-70%), UGT moderately reduced (-35%). High-first-pass drugs show drastically increased bioavailability.

str.note: Low in caudate-putamen; high in globus pallidus

cb.note: Purkinje, stellate, basket and granule cells

hip.note: Pyramidal cell axon initial segments; dentate gyrus

tha.note: Reticular nucleus only; absent from relay nuclei

hip.note: Dentate gyrus granule cells, with δ

substances.name: Diazepam
substances.indications: Anxiety, status epilepticus, muscle spasms, alcohol withdrawal (including acute agitation)

substances.name: Lorazepam
substances.indications: Status epilepticus (IV), acute agitation (IM rapid tranquillisation), acute panic/anxiety, insomnia, alcohol withdrawal

substances.name: Alprazolam
substances.indications: Panic disorder, generalised anxiety; high rebound and dependence potential

substances.name: Oxazepam
substances.indications: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal in patients with hepatic impairment

substances.name: Midazolam
substances.indications: Procedural sedation, anaesthesia induction, status epilepticus rescue, acute severe agitation (IM, off-label)

substances.name: Triazolam
substances.indications: Severe acute sleep-onset insomnia; dental conscious sedation

substances.name: Bretazenil
substances.indications: Investigational anxiolytic & anticonvulsant with reduced sedation, ataxia, tolerance, and dependence liability

substances.name: Zolpidem
substances.indications: Sleep-onset insomnia; less disruption of sleep architecture and less myorelaxation than BZDs at therapeutic doses

substances.name: Zopiclone / Eszopiclone
substances.indications: Insomnia (sleep onset and maintenance); bitter metallic dysgeusia common

substances.name: Flumazenil
substances.indications: Reversal of conscious sedation / BZD overdose; risk of acute withdrawal seizures
